title: Centaurorum et Lapitharum pugna
titleEn: The Centaurs and the Lapiths — Metamorphoses XII.210–377
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Nestor tells how Pirithous' wedding feast turned into a battle: the centaur Eurytus, drunk, seizes the bride, the other centaurs seize the other women, and Theseus wrenches her back and kills Eurytus with a mixing-bowl thrown in his face. From there the telling becomes a catalogue of killings, with altars, torches, table-legs, antlers and whole trees used as weapons, and this first piece breaks off with Peleus driving one thrust through the two chests of the centaur Demoleon.

advisory.lede: The fighting begins with the drunken centaurs seizing the bride and the other women at the wedding by force — a mass attempted rape that the Lapiths fight to stop.
advisory.more: At lines 222–225 Eurytus drags the bride Hippodame off by the hair while the other centaurs each seize whichever woman he wants or can lay hold of, and Ovid says the scene had the look of a city taken by storm. Theseus pulls her free at 231, and the rest of the part is the fighting that follows: a catalogue of killings told with unsparing physical detail, men crushed under a thrown altar and under a block of stone, blinded, set alight, and struck through the skull. Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Duxerat Hippodamen audaci Ixione natus,
nubigenasque feros positis ex ordine mensis
arboribus tecto discumbere iusserat antro.
sentences.l: Married had Hippodame the man born of bold Ixion, and the wild cloud-born ones, the tables set out in a row, he had bidden recline in a cave roofed over with trees.
sentences.i: The son of bold Ixion had married Hippodame, and had set the tables out in a row and bidden the wild cloud-born centaurs take their places in a cave roofed with trees.
sentences.n: audaci Ixione natus, literally “born from bold Ixion”, is a periphrasis for Pirithous, who is not named outright until 218. nubigenas, “cloud-born”, names the centaurs by their birth and stands as a noun. positis ex ordine mensis is an ablative absolute, “the tables having been set out in a row” — a noun and participle in the ablative doing the work of a whole clause; the construction recurs constantly in this battle.

sentences.t:
Haemonii proceres aderant, aderamus et ipsi,
festaque confusa resonabat regia turba.
sentences.l: Haemonian chiefs were present, present were we ourselves too, and the festal palace was resounding with the jumbled crowd.
sentences.i: The Thessalian chiefs were there, and we ourselves were there too, and the palace, dressed for the feast, rang with the milling crowd.
sentences.n: Haemonius is “Thessalian”, from Haemonia, the old name of Thessaly. aderamus et ipsi puts the narrator inside the scene, and the first person keeps returning through it (diximus 217, surgimus 227, vidi 327). confusa turba is an ablative of means with resonabat, “rang with the jumbled crowd”.

sentences.l: Look — they sing Hymenaeus, and the halls smoke with fires, and the bride is there, ringed by a throng of matrons and young wives; outstanding in face.
sentences.i: Look: they sing the wedding-hymn, the halls are smoky with torch-fire, and the bride comes in ringed by a crowd of matrons and young wives, conspicuous for her beauty.
sentences.n: Hymenaeon keeps the Greek accusative ending of the wedding-god's name; canunt Hymenaeon is “they sing Hymenaeus”, that is, the wedding-hymn. facie in praesignis facie is an ablative of respect, “outstanding in respect of face”. cincta ... caterva has its participle at the head of the line and the ablative it governs at the end.

sentences.t:
Felicem diximus illa
coniuge Pirithoum: quod paene fefellimus omen.
sentences.l: Fortunate we called Pirithous in that wife: and that omen we almost cheated.
sentences.i: We called Pirithous lucky in such a bride — and that word of good luck we came within a hair of proving false.
sentences.n: quod ... omen is a connecting relative: a relative pronoun opening a new sentence simply means “and that”, not “which”. It is a common Latin turn, and it opens clauses repeatedly in this part (quem 236, quos 311, quem 320). The omen is the lucky word just spoken (diximus); fallere omen is to make the spoken word turn out false, and paene says it nearly did.

sentences.t:
Nam tibi, saevorum saevissime Centaurorum,
Euryte, quam vino pectus, tam virgine visa
ardet, et ebrietas geminata libidine regnat.
sentences.l: For to you, cruellest of cruel Centaurs, Eurytus, as much as with wine your breast burns, so much with the maiden seen, and drunkenness doubled by lust rules.
sentences.i: For your breast, Eurytus, cruellest of the cruel Centaurs, burns as hot at the sight of the girl as it does with wine, and drunkenness doubled by lust takes command.
sentences.n: Ovid breaks off from narrating and speaks to the man himself — tibi with the vocative Euryte. This turning aside to address a character is apostrophe, and he does it again and again in this battle (Drya 296, Crenaee 313, Achille 363). tibi is a dative of possession with pectus, “the breast belonging to you”; quam ... tam correlate the two causes of the burning, and virgine visa is an ablative absolute used causally, “the maiden having been seen”.

sentences.t:
Protinus eversae turbant convivia mensae,
raptaturque comis per vim nova nupta prehensis.
sentences.l: At once the overturned tables throw the feasting into confusion, and the new bride is dragged by force, her hair seized.
sentences.i: At once the tables go over and the feast is in uproar, and the new bride is hauled off by force, dragged by the hair.
sentences.n: comis ... prehensis is another ablative absolute, its two words held apart across line 223 with per vim nova nupta packed between them. raptatur is the frequentative of rapio — not one snatch but repeated violent hauling.

sentences.t:
Eurytus Hippodamen, alii, quam quisque probabant,
aut poterant, rapiunt, captaeque erat urbis imago.
sentences.l: Eurytus Hippodame, the others each the woman whom they approved, or were able to, seize; and there was the look of a captured city.
sentences.i: Eurytus seizes Hippodame; the rest seize whichever woman each of them wanted, or could lay hold of — it looked like a city sacked.
sentences.n: One verb, rapiunt, serves both Eurytus and alii, and stands after both. quam quisque probabant is a relative clause with quisque, “whichever woman each man approved”, the verb plural by the sense of alii; aut poterant leaves rapere to be supplied. captae urbis imago compares the hall to a stormed town, where the seizing of the women was the expected sequel.

sentences.t:
Femineo clamore sonat domus: ocius omnes
surgimus, et primus “quae te vecordia,” Theseus
“Euryte, pulsat” ait, “qui me vivente lacessas
Pirithoum violesque duos ignarus in uno?”
sentences.l: With womanly outcry the house sounds: more swiftly we all rise, and first “What madness,” says Theseus, “strikes you, Eurytus, that with me living you should provoke Pirithous and wrong two men in one, not knowing it?”
sentences.i: The house rings with the women's screaming. We are all on our feet at once, and Theseus speaks first: “What madness is driving you, Eurytus, that with me alive you should provoke Pirithous and, without knowing it, wrong two men in one?”
sentences.n: ocius is a comparative adverb with nothing to compare it to, “all the quicker”. me vivente is an ablative absolute, “with me living”; qui ... lacessas ... violes has the subjunctive of characteristic after qui, “the kind of man to provoke”. duos in uno is the point of the challenge: to attack Pirithous is to attack Theseus with him, and ignarus grants that Eurytus does not know it.

sentences.t:
neve ea magnanimus frustra memoraverit ore,
submovet instantes raptamque furentibus aufert.
sentences.l: And that the great-hearted man might not have uttered these things with his mouth in vain, he pushes back those pressing on and carries the seized woman off from the raging ones.
sentences.i: And so that his great-hearted words should not have been spoken for nothing, he shoves back the ones crowding in and takes the stolen bride away from the maddened centaurs.
sentences.n: neve ... memoraverit is a negative purpose clause with the perfect subjunctive, “that he might not have spoken in vain”; the perfect looks back at the speech just finished. raptam is the participle used as a noun, “the seized woman”, and aufero takes a dative of the person robbed, here furentibus, “from the raging ones”.

sentences.t:
Ille nihil contra (neque enim defendere verbis
talia facta potest), sed vindicis ora protervis
insequitur manibus generosaque pectora pulsat.
sentences.l: He nothing in return — for he cannot defend such deeds with words — but the champion's face with insolent hands he goes after, and beats his noble breast.
sentences.i: He answers nothing — such deeds cannot be defended in words — but with brazen hands goes for the face of the man who stopped him, and pounds his noble chest.
sentences.n: Ille nihil contra has no verb at all: “says” must be supplied from the sense, a compression Latin allows and English will not. vindicis, “of the champion”, is Theseus, named at 237 by the patronymic Aegides; ille is Eurytus. ora and pectora are poetic plurals for one face and one chest.

sentences.t:
Forte fuit iuxta signis exstantibus asper
antiquus crater;
sentences.l: By chance there was close by, rough with figures standing out from it, an ancient mixing-bowl;
sentences.i: As it happened, there stood nearby an old mixing-bowl, rough with figures in relief;
sentences.n: signis exstantibus is an ablative of cause with asper, “rough by reason of the figures standing out” — relief-work on the bowl. asper closes line 235 and the noun it describes, crater, only arrives in the next line, so the adjective hangs over the line-end before it is resolved.

sentences.t:
quem vastum vastior ipso
sustulit Aegides adversaque misit in ora.
sentences.l: and this, huge as it was, one huger than the bowl itself — the son of Aegeus — lifted and sent into the face fronting him.
sentences.i: Huge as it was, the son of Aegeus, huger still, lifted it and flung it full in his face.
sentences.n: quem is a connecting relative opening the sentence, “and this”. The play is vastum ... vastior ipso: the bowl is huge, the man huger, with ipso an ablative of comparison. Aegides, “son of Aegeus”, is Theseus. Magnus prints vastior ipso, “huger than the bowl itself”; some editions print ipse, which would make it “himself huger”.

sentences.t:
Sanguinis ille globos pariter cerebrumque merumque
vulnere et ore vomens madida resupinus harena
calcitrat.
sentences.l: He, clots of blood and at once brain and unmixed wine, out of wound and out of mouth vomiting, on the soaked sand flat on his back, kicks.
sentences.i: He spews clots of blood, brain and neat wine together, out of the wound and out of his mouth, and lies on his back on the soaked sand, kicking.
sentences.n: globos sanguinis are lumps or clots, not a stream, and pariter puts the brain and the wine on the same footing as the blood. vulnere et ore is an ablative of the place from which, “out of the wound and out of the mouth”; madida harena is ablative too, sand already soaked by what he brings up. The one finite verb of the sentence, calcitrat, is held back to the first word of line 240, after two whole lines of participle.

sentences.t:
Ardescunt germani caede bimembres
certatimque omnes uno ore “arma, arma” loquuntur.
sentences.l: The two-formed brothers blaze up at the killing, and all of them, striving against one another, with one mouth say “arms, arms”.
sentences.i: His two-formed kinsmen catch fire at the killing, and every one of them, outdoing the next, shouts with one voice, “Weapons! Weapons!”
sentences.n: bimembres, “double-membered”, is the word for the centaurs' two bodily natures and stands here as a noun; germani marks them as the dead man's own kin. caede is an ablative of cause with ardescunt, an inceptive verb, “begin to blaze”. uno ore, “with one mouth”, is an ablative of manner.

sentences.t:
Vina dabant animos, et prima pocula pugna
missa volant fragilesque cadi curvique lebetes,
res epulis quondam, tum bello et caedibus aptae.
sentences.l: The wines were giving them courage, and in the first fighting cups, thrown, fly, and brittle jars and curved basins — things once for feasts, then fit for war and killings.
sentences.i: The wine was supplying the courage, and in the opening exchange the cups go flying, hurled, and fragile jars and round basins with them — gear meant once for dinner, now for war and slaughter.
sentences.n: prima pugna is an ablative of time, “in the first of the fighting”. missa agrees with pocula but covers the jars and basins as well: all three are thrown. res ... aptae stands in apposition to the whole list, and the contrast quondam ... tum, “once ... now”, is the joke — the tableware has changed employment.

sentences.t:
Primus Ophionides Amycus penetralia donis
haud timuit spoliare suis et primus ab aede
lampadibus densum rapuit funale coruscis,
sentences.l: First Amycus, Ophion's son, feared not to strip the inner shrine of its gifts, and first from the temple snatched a torch-stand thick with flickering lamps,
sentences.i: Amycus son of Ophion was the first not to shrink from stripping the inner shrine of its offerings, and the first to snatch from the temple a branched torch thick with flickering lights,
sentences.n: Ophionides is a Greek patronymic, “son of Ophion”. haud timuit spoliare is litotes — “was not afraid to” standing for “went boldly and did” — and the repeated primus ... primus makes him the first man to lay hands on sacred things. densum governs the ablative lampadibus ... coruscis, whose two words are set at the ends of line 247 with the verb between them.

sentences.t:
elatumque alte, veluti qui candida tauri
rumpere sacrifica molitur colla securi,
inlisit fronti Lapithae Celadontis et ossa
non cognoscendo confusa relinquit in ore.
sentences.l: and, raised high — as one who strains to break a bull's white neck with the sacrificial axe — he dashed it against the forehead of the Lapith Celadon and leaves the bones jumbled together in a face not to be known.
sentences.i: and, swinging it high like a man heaving up the sacrificial axe to break a bull's white neck, he smashed it into the forehead of Celadon the Lapith and left the bones mashed together in a face nobody could recognise.
sentences.n: elatum agrees with funale in the line before: the object carries over from the last unit. veluti qui ... molitur is a simile with an indefinite subject, “like a man who ...”, and molitur is the verb of heaving something with effort. non cognoscendo is a gerundive used as a plain adjective, “not to be recognised”, and confusa is “run together”, of bone that no longer holds its shape. The perfect inlisit and the present relinquit stand side by side — this alternation of past and vivid present runs through the whole battle.

sentences.t:
Exsiluere oculi, disiectisque ossibus oris
acta retro naris medioque est fixa palato.
sentences.l: The eyes sprang out, and, the bones of the face flung apart, the nose was driven backwards and fixed in the middle of the palate.
sentences.i: His eyes sprang from their sockets; the bones of his face flew apart, and his nose was driven back and lodged in the middle of his palate.
sentences.n: Exsiluere is the shortened poetic third-person plural perfect, the same as exsiluerunt; the ending recurs in this part (effugere 311, and beside it the full arserunt 275). disiectis ossibus oris is an ablative absolute. acta and fixa are both passive participles of the one subject naris, with the single est serving them both.

sentences.t:
Hunc pede convulso mensae Pellaeus acernae
stravit humi Pelates deiecto in pectora mento,
cumque atro mixtos sputantem sanguine dentes
vulnere Tartareas geminato mittit ad umbras.
sentences.l: Him, with a leg wrenched from a maple table, Pelates of Pella laid low on the ground, his chin driven down onto his chest, and him, spitting out teeth mingled with black blood, with the wound doubled he sends to the Tartarean shades.
sentences.i: Pelates of Pella knocked him to the ground with a leg torn off a maple table, his chin driven down into his chest, and while he was spitting out teeth mixed with black blood, doubled the wound and sent him to the shades of Tartarus.
sentences.n: Hunc is Amycus, who killed Celadon in the last unit and is killed in his turn here. pede ... mensae acernae is an ablative instrument with a genitive, “with a leg wrenched off a maple table”; deiecto ... mento is an ablative absolute, and geminato vulnere another ablative, “the wound having been doubled”, that is, by a second blow. cumque is the preposition cum with -que, going with atro ... sanguine, “mingled with black blood”, and not a temporal conjunction; sputantem is accusative, the object of mittit. The perfect stravit and the present mittit again stand in one sentence.

sentences.t:
Proximus ut steterat, spectans altaria vultu
fumida terribili “cur non” ait “utimur istis?”
sentences.l: As he had stood next in place, looking at the altars, smoking, with a terrible face, “Why do we not,” he says, “use these?”
sentences.i: Standing next in line, he looked at the smoking altars with a terrible face and said, “Why don't we use these?”
sentences.n: ut with the pluperfect steterat is temporal, “as he stood there”. Proximus is the centaur Gryneus, not named until 260. Two pairs are split across the line-end: altaria and vultu close 258, and their adjectives fumida and terribili open 259 in the same order. utor takes the ablative, so istis is “these things”, the altars he is looking at.

sentences.t:
cumque suis Gryneus inmanem sustulit aram
ignibus et medium Lapitharum iecit in agmen
depressitque duos, Brotean et Orion:
sentences.l: and with its own fires Gryneus lifted a monstrous altar and threw it into the middle of the Lapiths' column and crushed two, Broteas and Orios:
sentences.i: and Gryneus heaved up a huge altar, fire and all, hurled it into the middle of the Lapith ranks, and crushed two men under it, Broteas and Orios:
sentences.n: cum suis ignibus, “with its own fires”, keeps the altar burning as it flies, and the phrase is split by the line-end: cum ... suis stands at the head of 260 and its noun ignibus opens 261. medium ... in agmen is the Latin way of saying “into the middle of the column”: the adjective agrees with the noun rather than standing as a separate word for “middle”. Orion here is the Greek accusative of the centaur Orios, not the hunter.

sentences.t:
Orio
mater erat Mycale, quam deduxisse canendo
saepe reluctantis constabat cornua lunae.
sentences.l: To Orios the mother was Mycale, who, it was well established, had often drawn down by singing the horns of the resisting moon.
sentences.i: Orios' mother was Mycale, who was known to have drawn down the horns of the moon again and again by her singing, for all the moon's struggling.
sentences.n: Orio is a dative of possession, “the mother to Orios was Mycale”. constabat, “it was agreed”, governs an accusative and infinitive, quam ... deduxisse; canendo is a gerund in the ablative, “by singing”. reluctantis is genitive agreeing with lunae, “of the moon fighting back”, and cornua lunae are the horns of the crescent: the witch drags the moon out of the sky. Magnus prints reluctantis; some editions print the dative reluctanti.

sentences.t: “Non inpune feres, teli modo copia detur!”
sentences.l: “You will not carry it off unpunished — let only a chance at a weapon be given!”
sentences.i: “You will not get away with this — only let me find a weapon!”
sentences.n: non inpune feres is the standard threat, “you will not carry this off unpunished”. modo with the subjunctive detur is a wish used as a proviso, “if only a weapon be granted”; copia teli is “an opportunity of a weapon”, that is, anything to hand that will serve.

sentences.t:
dixerat Exadius telique habet instar, in alta
quae fuerant pinu votivi cornua cervi.
sentences.l: Exadius had said it, and he has the likeness of a weapon: the antlers of a votive stag, which had been on a tall pine.
sentences.i: So Exadius had said, and a weapon's equal came to hand: the antlers of a stag hung up as an offering on a tall pine.
sentences.n: instar is an indeclinable noun taking the genitive, “the equivalent of a weapon”. The relative clause is planted inside the phrase it belongs to: in alta ends line 266 and its noun pinu comes only after quae fuerant in 267, with the antecedent cornua following the clause altogether. Straightened out, the order is cornua cervi votivi, quae in alta pinu fuerant.

sentences.t:
Figitur hinc duplici Gryneus in lumina ramo
eruiturque oculos, quorum pars cornibus haeret,
pars fluit in barbam concretaque sanguine pendet.
sentences.l: With this Gryneus is pierced in the eyes by the double branch and is gouged as to his eyes, of which one part sticks on the antlers, part runs down onto his beard and hangs clotted with blood.
sentences.i: With that Gryneus is stabbed in the eyes by the forked antler and his eyes are torn out — part of them sticking to the tines, part running down into his beard and hanging there in clots of blood.
sentences.n: eruitur oculos is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive verb: the verb is passive, “he is gouged out”, and oculos names the part affected, “as to his eyes”. It is a Greek turn that Latin poets borrow, and it comes back twice more in this part (tectus ... malas 291, protectum pectora 351). quorum picks up oculos as an ordinary relative — not a connecting one, since it opens no new sentence — and its partitive genitive is divided between the two pars ... pars clauses; duplici ramo is the forked antler of the last unit.

sentences.t:
Ecce rapit mediis flagrantem Rhoetus ab aris
pruniceum torrem dextraque a parte Charaxi
tempora perstringit fulvo protecta capillo.
sentences.l: Look — Rhoetus snatches from the midst of the altars a blazing plum-wood brand, and on the right side grazes the temples of Charaxus, covered with tawny hair.
sentences.i: Look: Rhoetus snatches a blazing plum-wood brand from the middle of the altars and, on the right side, scrapes it across Charaxus' temples, covered as they are with tawny hair.
sentences.n: pruniceus is “of plum-wood” and torrem is the burning log itself. perstringit is “grazes, scrapes along”, a glancing blow — enough to set the hair alight, as the next lines show. Magnus prints perstringit; some editions print perfringit, “shatters”, which would make it a blow that breaks the skull instead. dextra a parte is an ablative, “on the right-hand side”.

sentences.t:
Correpti rapida, veluti seges arida, flamma
arserunt crines, et vulnere sanguis inustus
terribilem stridore sonum dedit,
sentences.l: Seized by the swift flame, like a dry cornfield, his hairs burned, and the blood seared in the wound gave a terrible sound with its hissing,
sentences.i: His hair caught the racing flame like a dry cornfield and burned, and the blood, seared in the wound, gave out a horrible hissing sound,
sentences.n: Correpti opens line 274 but its noun crines does not arrive until the next line, with the simile veluti seges arida dropped in between. arserunt is the full third-person plural perfect, standing beside the shortened forms used elsewhere in the part (exsiluere 252). stridore goes with terribilem, an ablative of cause: the hissing is what makes the sound terrible.

sentences.t:
ut dare ferrum
igne rubens plerumque solet, quod forcipe curva
cum faber eduxit, lacubus demittit:
sentences.l: as iron red with fire is generally wont to give, which, when the smith has drawn it out with the curved tongs, he lets down into the troughs:
sentences.i: the sound red-hot iron generally makes when the smith has lifted it out with his curved tongs and drops it into the trough:
sentences.n: dare has to borrow its object sonum from the clause before, “as red-hot iron is wont to give such a sound”. quod is the iron, object both of eduxit and of demittit; cum ... eduxit is “when he has drawn it out”, perfect indicative in a temporal clause, and lacubus is a dative of the goal, a poetic equivalent of in lacus.

sentences.t:
at illud
stridet et in tepida submersum sibilat unda.
sentences.l: but that thing screeches and, sunk in the warm water, hisses.
sentences.i: but the iron shrieks and, plunged under the warm water, hisses.
sentences.n: illud is the iron, picked up from quod in the clause before. Two verbs are given to the one noise, stridet and sibilat, with the participle submersum between them. Magnus prints tepida, “warm” — water already heated by the work; some editions print trepida, “agitated”.

sentences.t:
Saucius hirsutis avidum de crinibus ignem
excutit inque umeros limen tellure revulsum
tollit, onus plaustri, quod ne permittat in hostem,
ipsa facit gravitas:
sentences.l: The wounded man shakes the greedy fire out of his shaggy hair and lifts onto his shoulders a threshold wrenched up from the ground, a wagon's load; and that he should not launch it at his enemy the sheer weight itself brings about:
sentences.i: The wounded man beats the hungry fire out of his shaggy hair, and heaves onto his shoulders a doorstone torn up out of the earth, a wagon-load; and the sheer weight of it is what stops him from launching it at his enemy:
sentences.n: Saucius, “the wounded man”, is Charaxus, whose hair was set alight at 274–275. avidum ignem gives the flame an appetite of its own. onus plaustri stands in apposition to limen, “a wagon's load”. ne permittat is a substantive clause after facit, with quod, the stone, pulled out in front of it: “the weight brings it about that he does not launch it”; tellure revulsum is an ablative of separation, “torn away from the earth”.

sentences.t:
socium quoque saxea moles
oppressit spatio stantem propiore Cometen.
sentences.l: the stone mass crushed his comrade too, Cometes, standing at a nearer distance.
sentences.i: the block of stone crushed his own comrade as well, Cometes, who was standing too close.
sentences.n: quoque here is the plain adverb “also” — worth checking each time, since the same letters can be quo-que, “and with which”. spatio ... propiore is an ablative of the distance at which he stood, “at a closer range”, and the comparative has no second term expressed: closer than was safe. It is the comrade, not the enemy, whom the weight kills, which is the point the last two lines were building.

sentences.t:
Gaudia nec retinet Rhoetus: “Sic, conprecor,” inquit
“cetera sit fortis castrorum turba tuorum!”
sentences.l: And Rhoetus does not hold in his joy: “Thus, I pray,” he says, “may the rest of the crowd of your camp be brave!”
sentences.i: Rhoetus cannot contain his delight: “Just so,” he prays, “may the rest of your camp's crowd be brave!”
sentences.n: nec ... retinet is litotes for “lets it out”. sit is an optative subjunctive governed by conprecor, “I pray that the rest may be”; sic points back at what has just happened, and fortis, “brave” in the sense of the strength just shown, carries the sneer — may they all show their strength by killing their own.

sentences.t:
semicremoque novat repetitum stipite vulnus,
terque quaterque gravi iuncturas verticis ictu
rupit, et in liquido sederunt ossa cerebro.
sentences.l: and with the half-burnt log he renews the wound, gone at again, and three and four times with a heavy blow he broke the joinings of the crown, and the bones settled in the liquid brain.
sentences.i: and with the half-burnt log he opens the wound again, and three and four times with heavy blows he broke the sutures of the skull-top, and the bones settled down into the liquid brain.
sentences.n: repetitum vulnus is “the wound gone at a second time” and novat “makes it new”: Rhoetus returns to the head he had only grazed at 273. terque quaterque, “three times and four”, is the Latin way of saying “again and again”. iuncturas verticis are the joins between the plates of the skull at the crown. The present novat gives way to the perfects rupit and sederunt inside a single sentence.

sentences.t: Victor ad Euagrum Corythumque Dryantaque transit;
sentences.l: The victor passes on to Euagrus and Corythus and Dryas;
sentences.i: The winner moves on to Euagrus, Corythus and Dryas;
sentences.n: Victor is still Rhoetus, named by his role rather than his name. Dryanta is the Greek accusative of Dryas, as Brotean and Orion were at 262. The doubled -que ... -que strings the three names into a single list of intended victims, and the next lines take them one at a time.

sentences.t:
e quibus ut prima tectus lanugine malas
procubuit Corythus, “puero quae gloria fuso
parta tibi est?”
sentences.l: of whom, when Corythus fell forward, covered as to his cheeks with the first down, “What glory from a boy laid low has been got for you?”
sentences.i: and when Corythus went down among them, his cheeks covered with their first down, “What glory have you won from a boy struck down?”
sentences.n: e quibus is partitive, “of these three”. tectus ... malas is the Greek accusative of respect once more (as at 269), “covered in respect of his cheeks”: the first beard makes him barely more than a child. puero fuso is an ablative absolute doing the work of a cause, “a boy having been laid low”, and quae gloria ... parta tibi est is “what glory has been won for you”, tibi a dative of the person concerned.

sentences.t:
Euagrus ait, nec dicere Rhoetus
plura sinit rutilasque ferox in aperta loquentis
condidit ora viri perque os in pectora flammas.
sentences.l: says Euagrus; and Rhoetus does not let him say more, and fiercely into the open mouth of the man as he spoke buried the red flames, and through the mouth into his breast.
sentences.i: says Euagrus — and Rhoetus lets him say no more, but savagely drives the red flames into the open mouth of the man in mid-speech, and on through the mouth into his chest.
sentences.n: The object rutilas ... flammas is pulled apart from one end of the sentence to the other, rutilas in 294 and flammas the last word of 295, with everything else packed between. condidit is “buried, sank”, the verb of driving something in to its full depth, and the one verb governs both in aperta ora and per os in pectora. loquentis is a genitive participle agreeing with viri, “of the man as he was speaking”.

sentences.t:
Te quoque, saeve Drya, circum caput igne rotato
insequitur;
sentences.l: You too, savage Dryas, with fire whirled around your head, he goes after;
sentences.i: You too, savage Dryas, he goes for, whirling the fire round your head;
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside again to speak to the man Rhoetus is going after — te with the vocative Drya, a Greek form of the name, as with Eurytus at 219. Dryas is a Lapith, and the next unit says outright that he is the one target here who does not go down. igne rotato is an ablative absolute, “the fire having been whirled”, with circum caput sitting inside it.

sentences.t:
sed non in te quoque constitit idem
exitus:
sentences.l: but not in your case too did the same outcome hold:
sentences.i: but with you the ending was not the same:
sentences.n: quoque is again the adverb “also”, here inside the negative: “not in your case as well”, looking back to Corythus and Euagrus, who both died. constitit is “came to a stand, held good”, and idem exitus is the death that met the others. The sentence is the hinge of the episode: from here it is Rhoetus who is hurt.

sentences.t:
adsiduae successu caedis ovantem,
qua iuncta est umero cervix, sude figis obusta.
sentences.l: him, exulting at the success of unceasing slaughter, where the neck is joined to the shoulder, you pin with a fire-charred stake.
sentences.i: As he exulted in his unbroken run of killing, you pinned him where the neck joins the shoulder with a fire-hardened stake.
sentences.n: The address is still running: figis is second person and Dryas is the one spoken to, while ovantem is the object, Rhoetus. successu is an ablative of cause with ovantem, “exulting at the success”. qua is the relative adverb “at the point where”. sude ... obusta, the ablative of the instrument, is a stake with its end charred hard in fire, and its two words are split by the verb figis.

sentences.t:
Ingemuit duroque sudem vix osse revellit
Rhoetus et ipse suo madefactus sanguine fugit.
sentences.l: He groaned, and barely wrenched the stake out of the hard bone — Rhoetus — and himself, soaked with his own blood, flees.
sentences.i: Rhoetus groaned, worked the stake out of the hard bone with difficulty, and fled, drenched in his own blood.
sentences.n: The subject Rhoetus is held back to the head of 301, after two verbs have already run without him. duro ... osse is an ablative of separation with revellit; that form is the same for present and perfect, and beside the perfect ingemuit it reads as perfect here — some editions print the unambiguous revulsit. ipse marks the reversal: the man who soaked others is soaked now himself.

sentences.t:
Fugit et Orneus Lycabasque et saucius armo
dexteriore Medon et cum Pisenore Thaumas,
sentences.l: Orneus flees too, and Lycabas, and, wounded in the right shoulder, Medon, and Thaumas with Pisenor,
sentences.i: Orneus fled too, and Lycabas, and Medon with his right shoulder wounded, and Thaumas along with Pisenor,
sentences.n: One singular verb, fugit, heads a whole list of subjects: Latin lets the verb agree with the first name only and leaves the rest to follow. armus is the shoulder-blade of an animal, the right word for a centaur's forequarters, and it comes back at 377; dexteriore, a comparative used for the plain “right”, is cut off from armo by the line-end.

sentences.t:
quique pedum nuper certamine vicerat omnes
Mermeros (accepto tum vulnere tardius ibat!),
sentences.l: and he who lately in a contest of feet had beaten all, Mermerus — with the wound he had taken he was now going more slowly! —
sentences.i: and Mermerus, who not long before had beaten everyone in a foot-race (now, with a wound in him, he was moving rather slower!),
sentences.n: The relative clause runs ahead of the name it belongs to: quique ... vicerat omnes comes first and Mermeros only after it. pedum certamine is “a contest of feet”, a foot-race. accepto ... vulnere is an ablative absolute, “the wound having been taken”, and the comparative adverb tardius carries the joke that the exclamation mark points at.

sentences.t:
et Pholus et Melaneus et Abas praedator aprorum,
quique suis frustra bellum dissuaserat augur,
Astylos:
sentences.l: and Pholus and Melaneus and Abas the plunderer of boars, and the seer who had vainly argued his own people out of the war, Astylos:
sentences.i: and Pholus and Melaneus and Abas the boar-hunter, and the augur who had tried in vain to talk his own side out of the fight, Astylos:
sentences.n: praedator aprorum, “plunderer of boars”, stands in apposition as a hunter's title. The relative clause again runs ahead of the name it belongs to, just as with Mermerus at 304. dissuadeo takes a dative of the person advised, suis, “his own people”, and frustra says at once that they did not listen. Magnus prints the name Astylos; some editions print Asbolus.

sentences.t:
ille etiam metuenti vulnera Nesso
“ne fuge! ad Herculeos” inquit “servaberis arcus.”
sentences.l: He also said to Nessus, fearing wounds, “Do not flee! For the Herculean bows you will be kept.”
sentences.i: He also said to Nessus, who was afraid of being wounded, “Don't run! You will be kept for the bow of Hercules.”
sentences.n: ne fuge is a prohibition made with ne and the imperative, an old and poetic construction beside the prose noli fugere. metuenti ... Nesso is a dative with inquit, the participle agreeing with the name and separated from it by its own object vulnera. Herculeos arcus uses an adjective where English wants a genitive, “the bow of Hercules”, and the augur's words are a prophecy: Nessus will die by that bow, not here.

sentences.t:
At non Eurynomus Lycidasque et Areos et Imbreus
effugere necem:
sentences.l: But Eurynomus and Lycidas and Areos and Imbreus did not escape death:
sentences.i: But Eurynomus, Lycidas, Areos and Imbreus did not get away from death:
sentences.n: effugere here is not the infinitive but the shortened third-person plural perfect, effugerunt, the same ending as exsiluere at 252; the four nominative subjects make the reading certain. At non sets these four against the long list of those who did get away.

sentences.t:
quos omnes dextra Dryantis
perculit adversos.
sentences.l: and all these the right hand of Dryas struck down facing him.
sentences.i: Dryas' right hand struck them all down as they faced him.
sentences.n: quos is a connecting relative, “and all these”. adversos is predicative with the object: they died fronting him, not running — a detail the next sentence turns straight round with adversum ... vulnus.

sentences.t:
Adversum tu quoque, quamvis
terga fugae dederas, vulnus, Crenaee, tulisti;
sentences.l: A wound from in front you too, although you had given your back to flight, Crenaeus, took;
sentences.i: You too took your wound in front, Crenaeus, though you had turned your back and run;
sentences.n: Another turn aside to address the dying man, with the vocative Crenaee held back almost to the end of its own clause. The object adversum ... vulnus is split across the line-end, adversum in 312 and vulnus in the middle of 313, with everything else falling between. terga fugae dederas is the idiom “gave your back to flight”, that is, turned and ran, and quamvis with the indicative is normal in verse. The paradox is the point: he ran, and was still wounded from the front.

sentences.t:
nam grave respiciens inter duo lumina ferrum,
qua naris fronti committitur, accipis, imae.
sentences.l: for, looking back, you take the heavy iron between your two eyes, at the point where the nose is joined to the lowest brow.
sentences.i: for as you looked back you took the heavy iron between the eyes, at the point where the nose meets the bottom of the brow.
sentences.n: The address continues: accipis is second person. respiciens, “looking back”, is what turns the running man's face towards the weapon and so explains the wound in front. qua is again the relative adverb “at the point where”; imae agrees with the dative fronti, “to the lowest brow”, and is held back to the very last word of the line, away from its noun.

sentences.t:
In tanto fremitu cunctis sine fine iacebat
sopitus venis et inexperrectus Aphidas
languentique manu carchesia mixta tenebat,
fusus in Ossaeae villosis pellibus ursae.
sentences.l: In such an uproar, drowsed in all his veins without end and unwakened, Aphidas was lying, and in his slack hand was holding a mixed cup, sprawled on the shaggy skins of an Ossaean bear.
sentences.i: Through all that din Aphidas lay lulled to sleep in every vein, endlessly, and never woke; his slack hand still held a cup of mixed wine, and he sprawled on the shaggy hide of a bear from Ossa.
sentences.n: sopitus ... venis is “put to sleep in respect of all his veins”, the ablative naming the part affected, and sine fine goes with the sleeping, unbroken by the noise. carchesia mixta are cups of wine mixed with water, the ordinary way of drinking it. Ossaeae, of Mount Ossa in Thessaly, is separated from its noun ursae by the two words of the hide itself, villosis pellibus.

sentences.t:
Quem procul ut vidit frustra nulla arma moventem,
inserit amento digitos “miscenda” que dixit
“cum Styge vina bibes!”
sentences.l: When from afar he saw him stirring no weapons to no purpose, he puts his fingers into the throwing-strap and said, “Wine to be mixed with the Styx you shall drink!”
sentences.i: Seeing him from a distance not even uselessly waving a weapon, he hooks his fingers into the throwing-thong and said, “You'll be drinking your wine mixed with the Styx!”
sentences.n: Quem is a connecting relative, “and when he saw him”. frustra set beside nulla arma is pointed: the man is not even wasting effort, since he moves nothing at all. amentum is the leather loop wound round a javelin-shaft for the fingers. miscenda is a gerundive agreeing with vina, “wine that is to be mixed”, and cum Styge names the mixture — water from the river of the dead in place of the water in the cup.

sentences.t:
Phorbas; nec plura moratus
in iuvenem torsit iaculum, ferrataque collo
fraxinus, ut casu iacuit resupinus, adacta est.
sentences.l: — Phorbas; and delaying no longer he hurled the javelin at the young man, and the iron-shod ash was driven home into his neck, as he happened to be lying on his back.
sentences.i: So Phorbas; and without waiting longer he hurled the javelin at the young man, and the iron-tipped ash was driven into his neck as he lay there on his back.
sentences.n: The speaker's name comes only after his speech is over — the opposite arrangement from Euagrus ait at 293. fraxinus, “ash”, is the shaft named by the wood it is made of, with ferrata for the iron head. collo is a dative with adacta est, “driven home to the neck”, and casu, “by chance”, keeps the sleeper's posture accidental: he did not turn to meet it.

sentences.t:
Mors caruit sensu, plenoque e gutture fluxit
inque toros inque ipsa niger carchesia sanguis.
sentences.l: The death lacked feeling, and from the full throat flowed, and onto the couches and into the very cups, black blood.
sentences.i: He died without feeling it, and black blood flowed out of his brimming throat onto the couches and into the very cups.
sentences.n: careo takes the ablative: mors caruit sensu is “the death was without sensation”, since he never woke. The subject sanguis is held back to the last word of all, after both destinations have been named, and the repeated in ... in spreads the flow across them. ipsa carchesia are the same cups he was still holding at 318.

sentences.t:
Vidi ego Petraeum conantem tollere terra
glandiferam quercum;
sentences.l: I myself saw Petraeus trying to lift from the ground an acorn-bearing oak;
sentences.i: I saw Petraeus myself, trying to heave an acorn-bearing oak out of the ground;
sentences.n: Vidi ego brings the eyewitness back into his own story, as at aderamus 213: the whole battle is being reported by a man who was in it. terra is an ablative of separation with tollere, “to lift away from the ground”. glandifer, “acorn-bearing”, is a compound adjective of the high style.

sentences.t:
quam dum conplexibus ambit
et quatit huc illuc labefactaque robora iactat,
lancea Pirithoi costis inmissa Petraei
pectora cum duro luctantia robore fixit.
sentences.l: and while he goes about it with his arms and shakes it this way and that and tosses the loosened trunk, the lance of Pirithous, sent into Petraeus' ribs, pinned his breast, as it struggled with the hard oak.
sentences.i: and while he had his arms round it, shaking it this way and that and wrenching at the loosened trunk, Pirithous' lance, driven into Petraeus' ribs, pinned his straining chest to the hard wood.
sentences.n: quam is a connecting relative for the oak, object of ambit. dum with the present indicative is “while”, and it keeps the man's struggle going right up to the moment the spear arrives, the three verbs ambit, quatit and iactat all inside it. costis is a dative with inmissa, “sent into the ribs”; luctantia agrees with pectora and takes cum ... robore, “struggling with the hard trunk” — he is still wrestling the tree when the spear fixes him to it.

sentences.t:
Pirithoi cecidisse Lycum virtute ferebant,
Pirithoi virtute Chromin.
sentences.l: They kept saying that by Pirithous' valour Lycus had fallen, by Pirithous' valour Chromis.
sentences.i: They said Lycus fell by Pirithous' prowess, and Chromis by Pirithous' prowess.
sentences.n: ferebant, “they used to report”, governs an accusative and infinitive, cecidisse Lycum, with the same construction carried over to Chromin without a second verb. The phrase Pirithoi ... virtute is repeated exactly, split by the name in the first half and standing together in the second. Magnus prints the order Lycum virtute; some editions print virtute Lycum, the same words the other way about.

sentences.t:
Sed uterque minorem
victori titulum quam Dictys Helopsque dederunt:
sentences.l: But each of the two gave to the victor a lesser title than Dictys and Helops gave:
sentences.i: But the two of them brought the victor less credit than Dictys and Helops did:
sentences.n: uterque, “each of the two”, is singular in form and takes the plural dederunt here by the sense, since two men are meant. titulus is the “title” to fame that a killing earns, and minorem ... quam sets up the comparison the next lines pay off. victori is a dative of the person receiving.

sentences.t:
fixus Helops iaculo, quod pervia tempora fecit
et missum a dextra laevam penetravit ad aurem;
sentences.l: Helops was pierced by a javelin, which made his temples a passage and, sent from the right, drove through to the left ear;
sentences.i: Helops was run through by a javelin that made a passage of his temples: thrown from the right, it drove on through to the left ear;
sentences.n: fixus stands without est, which has to be supplied. pervia tempora fecit is “made the temples passable”, that is, bored a way clean through the head, and quod is the javelin, subject of both fecit and penetravit. missum agrees with quod, and a dextra, “from the right side”, is answered by laevam ... ad aurem at the other end of the sentence.

sentences.t:
Dictys, ab ancipiti delapsus acumine montis,
dum fugit instantem trepidans Ixione natum,
decidit in praeceps et pondere corporis ornum
ingentem fregit suaque induit ilia fractae.
sentences.l: Dictys, having slipped down from the two-pointed peak of the mountain while in panic he flees the son of Ixion pressing on him, fell headlong, and by the weight of his body broke a huge ash and drew his own guts onto the broken tree.
sentences.i: Dictys slipped from the mountain's twin-pointed crag as he fled in panic from Ixion's son at his heels, fell sheer down, broke a great ash tree with the weight of his body, and spitted his own guts on the broken trunk.
sentences.n: anceps acumen is a “two-headed point”, a forked crag, and ab ... delapsus is “having slipped down from”. Ixione natum is the same periphrasis as at 210, “the one born from Ixion”, that is Pirithous. dum with the present fugit fixes the flight as still going on at the moment of the fall. induit takes an accusative of the thing put on and a dative of what it is put onto: sua ilia ... fractae, “his own guts onto the broken tree”. pondere corporis is an ablative of means, and his own falling weight does both the breaking and the impaling.

sentences.t:
Victor adest Aphareus saxumque e monte revulsum
mittere conatur:
sentences.l: Aphareus is at hand as victor, and tries to throw a rock torn away from the mountain:
sentences.i: Aphareus arrives in triumph and tries to throw a rock he has wrenched from the mountain:
sentences.n: Victor stands in apposition to the name, “Aphareus is here, a victor”. e monte revulsum is an ablative of separation, “torn away out of the mountain”. Magnus prints Victor; some editions print Ultor, “as avenger”, which would make him come to pay a death back rather than fresh from a killing.

sentences.l: him as he throws the son of Aegeus forestalls with an oaken club, and breaks the huge bones of his elbow;
sentences.i: The son of Aegeus catches him in the act with an oak club and smashes the great bones of his elbow;
sentences.n: occupat is “gets in first”, the verb of forestalling: the blow lands before the throw can be made. mittentem is a participle used as the object, “the man in the act of throwing”, picking up mittere from the line before. ingentia is separated from its noun ossa by the verb frangit and by the line-end. Magnus prints mittentem; some editions print conantem, repeating the verb of trying instead of the verb of throwing.

sentences.t:
nec ulterius dare corpus inutile leto
aut vacat aut curat tergoque Bienoris alti
insilit haud solito quemquam portare nisi ipsum,
sentences.l: and he neither has leisure nor cares to give the useless body further to death, and leaps onto the back of tall Bienor, not accustomed to carry anyone except himself,
sentences.i: and he has neither the time nor the inclination to finish off the now useless body, but leaps onto the back of tall Bienor, who was not used to carrying anyone but himself,
sentences.n: vacat is used impersonally, “there is leisure”, and stands beside curat sharing the one infinitive dare: “he has neither time nor mind to”. corpus inutile is the man himself, made useless by the broken elbow. tergo is a dative with insilit, “leaps onto the back”. solito is dative and stands beside tergo, but the sense belongs to the centaur and not to his back: it is Bienor who is not used to carrying anyone. The indignity is the point: a centaur is now being ridden.

sentences.t:
opposuitque genu costis prensamque sinistra
caesariem retinens vultum minitantiaque ora
robore nodoso praeduraque tempora fregit:
sentences.l: and he set his knee against the ribs, and, holding with his left the hair he had seized, with the knotted oak he broke his face and threatening mouth and rock-hard temples:
sentences.i: and he braced his knee against the ribs and, gripping the seized hair with his left hand, smashed the face, the threatening mouth and the rock-hard temples with his knotted club:
sentences.n: costis is a dative with opposuit, “set against the ribs”. prensam ... caesariem is split by sinistra and the line-end, the noun opening 348; sinistra is an ablative with manu left to be understood, “with the left”. The one verb fregit governs three objects, vultum, ora and tempora, and robore nodoso is the ablative instrument — the same oak club used at 342.

sentences.t:
robore Nedymnum iaculatoremque Lycopen
sternit et inmissa protectum pectora barba
Hippason et summis exstantem Riphea silvis
Thereaque,
sentences.l: with the club he lays low Nedymnus and Lycopes the javelin-man, and Hippasus, protected as to his breast by a beard let down over it, and Rhipheus, standing out above the topmost woods, and Thereus,
sentences.i: With the same club he brings down Nedymnus and Lycopes the javelin-thrower, and Hippasus, whose chest was screened by a beard flowing down over it, and Rhipheus, who stood clear of the tree-tops, and Thereus,
sentences.n: robore repeats the robore that opened 349 in the last unit, carrying the one club through four more killings. protectum ... pectora is the Greek accusative of respect again (as at 269 and 291), “protected in respect of the chest”, with inmissa ... barba the ablative of means. summis ... silvis is an ablative with exstantem, “rising clear of the topmost woods”, a measure of the centaur's height.

sentences.t:
Haemoniis qui prensos montibus ursos
ferre domum vivos indignantesque solebat.
sentences.l: who used to carry home bears caught in the Haemonian mountains, alive and indignant.
sentences.i: the man who used to carry bears home from the Thessalian mountains alive and furious.
sentences.n: Haemoniis ... montibus is an ablative of place, “in the Thessalian mountains”, its two words set round qui prensos. vivos and indignantes are predicative with ursos: he brought them home still alive and still fighting him. solebat with ferre makes it his regular habit, not a single feat.

sentences.t:
Haud tulit utentem pugnae successibus ultra
Thesea Demoleon:
sentences.l: Demoleon did not bear it that Theseus should use his successes in the fight any further:
sentences.i: Demoleon could not endure Theseus pressing his run of success in the fight any longer:
sentences.n: haud tulit takes the accusative participle utentem ... Thesea, “did not put up with Theseus making use of”, and utor governs the ablative successibus. Thesea is the Greek accusative of the name; it is separated from its participle by the line-end, and the subject Demoleon arrives last of all.

sentences.t:
solido divellere dumo
annosam pinum magno molimine temptat;
sentences.l: from the solid thicket to tear away an aged pine with great effort he tries;
sentences.i: He tries, with a great heave, to wrench an aged pine out of the solid thicket;
sentences.n: The infinitive divellere is held apart from temptat, which governs it, by the whole of the line-end and the object annosam pinum between. solido ... dumo is an ablative of separation, the thicket the tree is torn from, and magno molimine an ablative of manner, “with a great effort”. Magnus prints solido divellere dumo; some editions print solidoque revellere trunco, “to wrench it away from the solid trunk”.

sentences.t: quod quia non potuit, praefractam misit in hostem.
sentences.l: and since he could not do that, he sent it, snapped off short, at his enemy.
sentences.i: and since he could not manage it, he snapped it off and threw it at his enemy.
sentences.n: quod is a connecting relative used as the object of potuit, “because he could not do this”, with facere left to be supplied. praefractam agrees with pinum from the line before, “broken off short in front”: the tree gives way part-way, and the broken piece becomes the missile.

sentences.t:
Sed procul a telo Theseus veniente recessit
Pallados admonitu: credi sic ipse volebat.
sentences.l: But far from the weapon as it came Theseus drew back, at Pallas' warning: so he himself wished it to be believed.
sentences.i: But Theseus stepped well clear of the weapon as it came, warned by Pallas — or so he himself liked it to be believed.
sentences.n: a telo ... veniente is split round the name Theseus: “from the weapon while it was on its way”. Pallados is the Greek genitive of Pallas, with admonitu an ablative of cause, “by the warning of Pallas”. credi is a passive infinitive after volebat, and the narrator's aside quietly declines to vouch for the goddess's part: that was what Theseus wanted believed.

sentences.t:
Non tamen arbor iners cecidit; nam Crantoris alti
abscidit iugulo pectusque umerumque sinistrum.
sentences.l: Yet the tree did not fall inert; for from the throat of tall Crantor it cut away his breast and his left shoulder.
sentences.i: Even so the tree did not fall to no purpose: it sheared away tall Crantor's chest and left shoulder from the throat.
sentences.n: iners, “doing nothing, without effect”, is predicative with cecidit. iugulo is an ablative of separation with abscidit, “cut off from the throat”, and the genitive Crantoris alti is held over the line-end, waiting for the two nouns pectus and umerum in the next line.

sentences.t:
Armiger ille tui fuerat genitoris, Achille,
quem Dolopum rector, bello superatus, Amyntor
Aeacidae dederat pacis pignusque fidemque.
sentences.l: He had been the armour-bearer of your father, Achilles — whom Amyntor, ruler of the Dolopians, beaten in war, had given to the son of Aeacus as pledge and warrant of peace.
sentences.i: He had been your father's armour-bearer, Achilles — Amyntor, king of the Dolopes, beaten in war, had handed him over to the son of Aeacus as a pledge and guarantee of peace.
sentences.n: The narrator turns and addresses his listener: tui ... genitoris with the vocative Achille. This is the same figure used on the fighters themselves (Eurytus 219, Dryas 296, Crenaeus 313), but here it is aimed outside the story, at the man being told it. quem is a connecting relative for Crantor. Aeacidae, “to the son of Aeacus”, is Peleus, Achilles' father, who acts in the very next lines. pignus and fidem are predicative accusatives with dederat, “gave him as pledge and warrant” — the hostage handed over to seal a settlement.

sentences.t:
Hunc procul ut foedo disiectum vulnere Peleus
vidit, “at inferias, iuvenum gratissime Crantor,
accipe” ait, validoque in Demoleonta lacerto
fraxineam misit, mentis quoque viribus, hastam.
sentences.l: When from afar Peleus saw him torn open by the hideous wound, “But take these offerings to the dead, Crantor, most beloved of young men,” he says, and with strong upper arm at Demoleon he sent the ashen spear — with the strength of his mind too.
sentences.i: When Peleus saw him from a distance ripped open by that hideous wound, “Take these death-offerings, Crantor, dearest of young men,” he says, and hurled the ash spear at Demoleon with a strong arm — and with the strength of his mind behind it too.
sentences.n: Hunc is Crantor, with disiectum, “flung apart”, agreeing with it. inferiae are the offerings owed to a dead man: killing his killer is the gift Peleus sends him, and gratissime Crantor is a vocative addressed to a corpse. lacertus is the upper arm, here an ablative of means, and mentis viribus is added after it to set the mind's force beside the arm's. Magnus prints mentis quoque viribus; some editions print contentis ... viribus, “with strength strained to the full”.

sentences.t:
Quae laterum cratem praerupit et ossibus haerens
intremuit.
sentences.l: It smashed through the wickerwork of the sides and, sticking in the bones, quivered.
sentences.i: It broke through the cage of the ribs and stood quivering, lodged in the bone.
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative for hasta, “and this spear”. laterum cratem, “the hurdle-work of the flanks”, sees the rib-cage as woven wicker. ossibus is a dative with haerens, “clinging to the bones”, and intremuit stands alone at the head of 371, the verb held over the line-end so that the shaft is still quivering as the sentence ends.

sentences.t:
Trahit ille manu sine cuspide lignum
(id quoque vix sequitur), cuspis pulmone retenta est.
sentences.l: He drags out with his hand the wood without its point — even that comes only barely — the point is held back in the lung.
sentences.i: He drags the shaft out by hand, without the head — and even that comes only just — while the head is held fast in the lung.
sentences.n: sine cuspide lignum is the shaft that comes away headless, the point named separately at the end. id quoque is the adverb “even that”, not the relative quo-que: pulling the bare wood out is hard enough. sequitur is used of the shaft “coming away” when it is tugged, and retenta est, “was held back”, sets the point against it, kept behind in the lung.

sentences.t:
Ipse dolor vires animo dabat: aeger in hostem
erigitur pedibusque virum proculcat equinis.
sentences.l: The pain itself was giving strength to his spirit: sick, against his enemy he rears up and tramples the man with his horse's feet.
sentences.i: The pain itself gave his spirit strength: wounded as he was, he reared up at his enemy and trampled the man with his horse's hooves.
sentences.n: Ipse dolor is the wound's own pain, made the source of the strength, with animo a dative, “to his spirit”. aeger, “sick, wounded”, is predicative with erigitur, and that passive is used in the middle sense, “raises himself upright”. pedibus ... equinis is what a centaur has to trample with — the horse half of him doing the work.

sentences.t:
Excipit ille ictus galea clipeoque sonanti
defensatque umeros praetentaque sustinet arma
perque armos uno duo pectora perforat ictu.
sentences.l: He catches the blows on helmet and clanging shield and guards his shoulders and holds up his weapons stretched out before him, and through the shoulder-blades pierces two breasts with one stroke.
sentences.i: Peleus takes the blows on his helmet and ringing shield, protects his shoulders, holds his weapons out in front of him, and with one thrust drives clean through the shoulder-blades and pierces both chests.
sentences.n: ille is Peleus, who threw the spear; excipit is “receives, catches” a blow on the armour, and praetenta arma are the weapons held out in front as a guard. The two words for shoulder are kept apart: umeros in 376 are Peleus' own, armos in 377 the shoulder-blades of the horse-body, the same word used of Medon's wound at 302. duo pectora is the point of the line: a centaur has a man's chest and a horse's chest, and uno ... ictu takes the thrust through both. Magnus prints clipeo ... sonanti, the shield ringing; some editions print sonantes, which would attach the ringing to the blows instead.
